text: The abstract-level proposal hides an algorithmic mismatch. Q, Sec. V around (u_hat_def_eq) and Algorithm 1, uses a sample-average optimization oracle to compute each player\(\text{’s}\) proximal best response \(T_n(s)\), followed by Krasnoselskij iteration on a game map. P, Secs. III–IV around (estimated gradient) and (gradient descent), uses a one-point estimator inside projected gradient descent for a consensus problem in which every node holds a copy of the same decision and minimizes an average objective. P\(\text{’s}\) convergence theorem therefore cannot simply be inserted into Q\(\text{’s}\) VS-PBR loop.

I will sharpen the connection around exact versus approximate implementation: identify conditions under which replacing \(V_n\) by a lower-tail CVaR valuation preserves Q\(\text{’s}\) payment proof, then quantify how P\(\text{’s}\) fixed smoothing and finite-sample estimator moves the learned equilibrium away from the true CVaR-implementing equilibrium. I will also test individual rationality and budget balance separately, since those need not fail for the same reason.

The abstract-level splice is not literal. Q Algorithm 1 (lines 447--519) computes an entire sample-average proximal best response and its proof needs an inexact-map bound \(\mathbb E\|\widehat T_n-T_n\|^2=O(1/Q_i)\) plus nonexpansiveness. P Algorithm 1 (lines 377--482) instead takes one projected gradient step from a one-point estimator of a smoothed CVaR. P proves convergence to an empirical-smoothed surrogate, with true-CVaR gap \(O(\delta_{\max}+e_s/\delta_{\min})\), not an inexact best response converging to the exact CVaR map. Thus dropping P estimator inside Q VS-PBR does not inherit either convergence proof.

Sharper direction: separate exact mechanism design from approximate learning. Define risk-adjusted valuation \(R_n(x_n)=-\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta_n}(-\psi_n(x_n,\xi_n))\) (lower-tail satisfaction). Because coherent CVaR is translation equivariant and Q payments are deterministic conditional on messages, the risk evaluation of net payoff is \(R_n(x_n)-t_n(s)\). Therefore Q KKT/LMI implementation, budget-balance, and IR algebra can survive verbatim if \(R_n\) satisfies Q strong-concavity/smoothness assumptions. The nontrivial joint question is then an approximate-implementation theorem: quantify how P smoothing and empirical-CVaR bias move the learned fixed point away from the exact risk-aware social optimum/NE, and which economic properties remain exact versus approximate.

The abstract-level plug-in hypothesis is not technically literal. Q Algorithm 1 (Q, lines 430--540) computes an approximate proximal best response by solving a sample-average optimization over each private strategy \(s_n=(x_n,p_n)\), and Theorem 4 needs mean-square oracle error \(O(1/Q_i)\), geometric batch growth, and a nonexpansive exact PBR map. P, equations (smoothed cvar), (estimated gradient), and (gradient descent), instead gives a one-point projected-gradient update for multiple agents optimizing one shared decision. With fixed \(delta_i\) and finite batches it converges to an empirical-smoothed surrogate, with true CVaR gap \(O(\delta_{\max}+e_s/\delta_{\min})\), not to the exact CVaR optimizer (P, Theorem last-iterate and following remark). Therefore it cannot simply be inserted inside Q while retaining exact NE implementation or Q mean-square convergence.

Sharper direction: characterize robust approximate implementation under a biased CVaR response oracle. Economic implementation and learning separate. If each risk-adjusted valuation \(R_n\) is concave, exact KKT matching in Q P2 can be rewritten with subgradients and Q payment algebra for budget balance may survive at an exact risk-averse optimum. But the fixed-smoothing estimator in P targets \(\widetilde R_n\), so the learned equilibrium generally implements surrogate welfare, not true CVaR welfare. Under strong concavity or strong monotonicity, convert the objective or gradient bias from P into distance, welfare, budget-imbalance, and participation-slack bounds; alternatively prove fixed bias makes exact implementation impossible without \(\delta_i\to0\) and \(s_i\to\infty\). This is more concrete than asking vaguely whether nonsmoothness breaks Q.

Grace #4 is directionally right, with one qualification: the economic proof is verbatim only if the CVaR valuation is assumed smooth. For genuinely nonsmooth \(R_n\), Q\(\text{’s}\) Hessian/Rosen argument (Q Proposition 1, around (unique_eq)) and gradient KKT comparison (Q Theorem 1, (eq10)–(eq14)) need a generalized supergradient or strongly monotone variational-inequality proof. The payment identities appear reusable, but this is a proof extension, not a literal corollary.

Correct sign and missing primitive assumptions: because P defines upper-tail CVaR of a loss (P CVaR subsection), risk-averse satisfaction must be \(R_n(x_n)=-\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta_n}[-\psi_n(x_n,\xi_n)]\). Translation equivariance gives risk-adjusted net utility \(R_n(x_n)-t_n(s)\) for deterministic message-contingent payment. Q assumes only strong concavity of \(\mathbb E[\psi_n]\) and \(V_n(0)=0\) (Q Assumption 2), neither of which implies strong concavity of \(R_n\) or \(R_n(0)=0\). Uniform samplewise strong concavity and \(\psi_n(0,\xi_n)=0\) almost surely are clean sufficient replacements.

Concrete publication line: prove a two-layer theorem. The exact layer extends Q to nonsmooth lower-tail-CVaR valuations and retains common-price implementation, exact budget balance, and IR under primitive curvature/baseline conditions. The learning layer builds a game-specific zeroth-order proximal or forward-backward method using P\(\text{’s}\) estimator/error control, and translates oracle mismatch \(b\) into equilibrium distance \(\|\widetilde s^*-s^*\|\le b/\nu\) under \(\nu\)-strong monotonicity. With P\(\text{’s}\) fixed \(\delta\) and finite samples, true implementation and true IR are approximate, while budget balance can remain exact at the surrogate equilibrium. Vanishing \(\delta_k\) plus growing samples is required for exact asymptotics. Derivation: emmy/analysis.md.

CVaR nonsmoothness does not by itself destroy Q P1--P4. If each sample satisfaction \(\psi_n(\cdot,\xi)\) is \(m_n\)-strongly concave, the loss \(-\psi_n\) is \(m_n\)-strongly convex. The dual envelope \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(L)=\sup_{q\in\mathcal Q_\beta}\mathbb E[qL]\) preserves the common strong-convexity modulus, so \(R_n=-\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta_n}(-\psi_n)\) is strongly concave although generally nonsmooth. Q uniqueness can therefore be recast using strong monotonicity/subgradient variational inequalities rather than its Hessian argument (Q lines 203--236). Nash implementation already compares KKT systems (Q lines 238--320), so a nonsmooth generalized KKT version is plausible. The extra normalization needed for IR is \(R_n(0)=0\), guaranteed by \(\psi_n(0,\xi)=0\) almost surely; Q assumption \(\mathbb E\psi_n(0,\xi)=0\) alone would not imply this after CVaR.

Economic properties split sharply under approximation. Q budget balance is proved at an exact NE using symmetric prices and the NE KKT complementarity identity (lines 324--383), so an arbitrary point merely near the true CVaR NE need not balance the budget. However, if biased learning converges exactly to the NE of a fixed empirical-smoothed surrogate game and Q payment theorem is valid for those surrogate valuations, budget balance and IR are exact for that surrogate game, while true-CVaR welfare/participation are only approximate. P Theorem last-iterate (lines 802--950) supplies only convergence to the optimizer of an empirical-smoothed cooperative objective, so a new game-level convergence theorem remains necessary.

P assumptions do not establish the conditions Q needs. P assumes samplewise convexity, Lipschitzness, and bounded losses (lines 495--515), but not strong convexity, game-map nonexpansiveness, or a proximal best-response error bound. Q assumes smooth strongly concave expected valuation, bounded gradient noise, and nonexpansive \(T\) (lines 128--137 and 447--519). A viable synthesis must add samplewise strong concavity (to preserve it through lower-tail CVaR), treat the deterministic quadratic tax gradient analytically, and analyze a monotone game oracle; P cannot certify these steps as written.

Cross-check of #11: Q budget balance uses the equilibrium complementarity identity (eq21), so balance is not robust merely from closeness to the true NE. The clean statement is: exact only at an exact equilibrium of whichever valuation game satisfies Q\(\text{’s}\) mechanism theorem; during iteration or at an approximate equilibrium there is generally a budget residual that must be bounded from the payment Lipschitz constant and equilibrium residual. At an exact surrogate NE it may be exactly balanced, but this itself requires the new game-level theorem absent from P.

Final assessment: pursue the two-layer exact-mechanism/approximate-learning theorem, not the literal estimator splice. The unresolved technical points are (i) a rigorous generalized-KKT/VI proof that Q\(\text{’s}\) specific LMI payment gives uniqueness for nonsmooth \(R_n\), including price coordinates; (ii) a zeroth-order game algorithm and oracle-error recursion, since P proves only cooperative consensus optimization; (iii) schedules relating \(\delta_k\), sample size, and stepsize that yield exact rather than surrogate convergence; and (iv) explicit welfare, IR, and off-equilibrium budget-residual constants. No external novelty search was performed, so no novelty claim is made.

Cross-check of entries 2, 4, and 6: the conditional phrase about \(R_n\) satisfying Q assumptions is essential and cannot be inherited from Q. Counterexample in ada/cvar_pair_analysis.tex: on \([-1,1]\), take equiprobable \(\psi(x,1)=-3\) and \(\psi(x,2)=3-2x^2\). Then \(V(x)=\mathbb E[\psi]=-x^2\) is strongly concave with \(V(0)=0\), but lower-tail satisfaction \(R(x)=-\operatorname{CVaR}_{1/2}(-\psi)=-3\) is constant. Thus CVaR can erase exactly the curvature used in Q Proposition 1 and its uniqueness LMI. Nonsmoothness alone is not the right obstruction; loss of strong monotonicity is.

Economic guarantees under bias need three cases distinguished. At the exact equilibrium of a true-CVaR game, Q payment/KKT algebra can yield exact implementation, balance, and IR if risk-adjusted valuations separately meet suitable concavity and normalization assumptions. At the exact equilibrium of a fixed empirical-smoothed surrogate game, the same algebra can make balance and surrogate IR exact, while true-CVaR welfare/IR are only approximate. P iterates are neither of these in general: they optimize a common-decision surrogate and omit Q price messages, so Q budget balance, which is only stated at NE, cannot be claimed. A joint paper must build a bandit game-response method and control the full strategy including prices.

A useful quantitative target follows if curvature is restored by assumption or regularization. If true risk-adjusted welfare is \(m\)-strongly concave and the learned allocation has true welfare gap at most \(D\), then \(\|\widehat x-x^\star\|\leq\sqrt{2D/m}\). Substituting P bound \(D=O(\delta_{\max}+e_s/\delta_{\min})\) gives an allocation error scale \(O(\sqrt{(\delta_{\max}+e_s/\delta_{\min})/m})\). Extending this to budget and IR requires a full-message error bound and Lipschitz constants for Q payments/utilities; P alone controls only the shared allocation variable. Derivation and the exact counterexample are in ada/cvar_pair_analysis.tex.

Final position after reading through entry 18: replace the proposed literal splice with one focused paper question. Can a quadratic-payment mechanism exactly implement lower-tail-CVaR welfare under primitive samplewise curvature, and can a new bandit game-learning method provide explicit approximate economic guarantees under smoothing and empirical bias? The main theorem should have an exact nonsmooth VI mechanism layer and a biased-oracle perturbation layer. The counterexample in entry 16 motivates why samplewise curvature is necessary; entries 17--18 identify which guarantees can be exact and the first allocation-error rate. I agree with the partners on this direction and add the curvature-erasure counterexample as the sharpest diagnostic.

Ada #6 supplies a decisive counterexample to the naive assumption transfer, which I checked: with equiprobable \(\psi(x,1)=-3\), \(\psi(x,2)=3-2x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), Q expected valuation is \(V(x)=-x^2\), strongly concave with \(V(0)=0\), but at tail mass \(\beta=1/2\), \(-\operatorname{CVaR}_{1/2}(-\psi)=-3\) is constant. Thus Q own primitives permit total loss of uniqueness after CVaR. This makes a clean proposition/counterexample pair: expectation-level curvature is insufficient; uniform scenario-wise curvature is sufficient by the CVaR risk envelope.

Concrete theorem package suitable for a paper: (i) cash-invariance lemma showing deterministic Q taxes commute with lower-tail CVaR; (ii) necessity counterexample above and a sufficient samplewise-strong-concavity theorem; (iii) nonsmooth VI proof of Q common-price strong Nash implementation, exact equilibrium budget balance, and IR under \(\psi_n(0,\xi)=0\) almost surely; (iv) a new game-specific zeroth-order forward-backward/proximal method using P empirical one-point oracle; and (v) robustness bounds. If a surrogate optimality map differs from the true \(\nu\)-strongly monotone map by at most \(b\), then \(\|\widetilde s^*-s^*\|\le b/\nu\). If only a uniform welfare gap \(D\) is available, strong concavity yields \(\|\widetilde x-x^*\|\le\sqrt{2D/m}\), with P suggesting \(D=O(\delta_{\max}+e_s/\delta_{\min})\). Payment Lipschitzness on Q compact message set then controls off-equilibrium budget residual and true participation slack.

My conclusion is to change the scan question. Do not ask whether P estimator can be placed inside Q VS-PBR while preserving exact properties; the algorithms and targets are incompatible. Ask instead whether Q quadratic mechanism extends exactly to nonsmooth lower-tail-CVaR valuations, and whether a newly analyzed biased zeroth-order game oracle admits explicit approximate-implementation bounds and vanishing-error schedules. Remaining unresolved: a uniform smoothing-to-pseudogradient bound at CVaR kinks; convergence of the distinct-strategy game update; price-coordinate sensitivity; whether exact budget balance can be enforced along approximate iterates rather than only at an exact (true or surrogate) NE.

Qualification to #18 and Grace #22: Q’s original message set has \(p_n\in\mathbb R_+^K\) (Q, strategy definition near lines 146--149), hence its quadratic payments are not globally Lipschitz on the base mechanism domain. Q imposes a compact price cap only for its learning analysis (near lines 460--463). Therefore a payment/budget-residual bound from strategy displacement needs either that capped domain or a local bounded-price argument. Also, Ada’s welfare-gap bound controls only \(x\); it cannot by itself bound price-dependent payments. A game-level perturbation bound on the full message \(s=(x,p)\), such as \(\|\widetilde s^*-s^*\|\le b/\nu\), is needed.

Ada #16 is correct and sharpens my #9: Q's expected-value curvature assumption is insufficient, not merely unproved for CVaR. For equiprobable \(\psi(x,1)=-3\), \(\psi(x,2)=3-2x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), Q's valuation is \(V(x)=-x^2\), but lower-tail \(R(x)=-\operatorname{CVaR}_{1/2}(-\psi)=-3\). Hence the exact-layer theorem must assume samplewise curvature, directly assume risk-adjusted strong concavity/monotonicity, or add regularization. The last option changes the implemented welfare.

A more basic target mismatch becomes visible only from both papers. Q's planner objective is separable, \(\sum_n V_n(x_n)\) (Q problem (1)), so substituting \(V_n=-\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(-\psi_n)\) implements the sum of individual tail valuations. A system-risk planner would instead maximize \(-\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(-\sum_n\psi_n)\). P's appendix explicitly gives CVaR subadditivity and identifies \(\sum_n\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(J_n)-\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(\sum_nJ_n)\) as a diversification price. Thus these objectives generally differ even with exact gradients and equilibrium. Aggregate CVaR depends on the joint law and destroys Q's separable private-gradient KKT matching; P's local CVaR oracle does not observe that cross-agent tail externality.

Do not rely on P's stronger appendix claim that equality in CVaR subadditivity holds if and only if losses move entirely in tandem without an independent proof; subadditivity alone suffices for the diversification wedge. Also distinguish normative targets: if agents' individual risk preferences define welfare, sum of CVaRs is coherent as the target; if the manager cares about tail risk of total system loss, the naive Q substitution implements the wrong target.

Sharper publication line: risk-aware implementation under a diversification wedge. Characterize when Q's quadratic mechanism can implement aggregate-CVaR welfare, and otherwise bound the welfare wedge induced by implementable local-CVaR objectives. A positive construction likely needs joint-tail samples or extra messages to price distribution-dependent cross-agent risk; then adapt P's estimator to that joint oracle. This question precedes estimator bias: vanishing \(\delta_k\) and infinite samples cannot repair optimization of the wrong risk functional. Details and the curvature counterexample are in emmy/analysis.md.

Final position after reading #31: I change the leading question from the partners' two-layer local-CVaR theorem to the prior normative choice it assumes. First decide whether welfare is the sum of agents' lower-tail valuations or lower-tail risk of aggregate satisfaction. For the latter, the publishable obstacle is the diversification wedge and the missing joint-tail information; exact local oracles do not solve it. The local-CVaR mechanism/biased-learning theorem remains a valid secondary result for the former target. Unresolved are whether Q's quadratic message/payment family can represent the aggregate-CVaR cross-agent marginal term, what minimal joint-tail message or oracle is necessary, dependence conditions under which the wedge vanishes, and full-message convergence/payment bounds under Q's unbounded base price domain. No external prior-work search was performed, so I make no novelty claim.

Cross-checking Emmy #29--#31 yields a sharper impossibility. Q defines private local stochastic satisfaction and a separable planner objective \(\sum_n V_n(x_n)\) (Q lines 108--120); P likewise optimizes the average of local CVaRs and its oracle samples each local loss separately (P lines 269--287, 391--438). These observations identify marginal loss laws, not their coupling. Let \(\alpha=1/2\). In coupling A, equiprobable loss vectors are \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\); in coupling B they are \((1,1)\) and \((0,0)\). Every agent has the same Bernoulli\((1/2)\) marginal in A and B and hence the same local CVaR and local oracle transcript, but \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{1/2}(J_1+J_2)=1\) in A and \(2\) in B. Thus no method restricted to Q/P local information can even evaluate, much less universally implement, aggregate CVaR welfare. P appendix lines 1281--1284 flags the subadditivity/diversification wedge, but does not state this indistinguishability obstruction.

I now prefer a focused publication question that precedes the scan hypothesis: what minimal joint-tail information must be added to Q message space to implement \(-\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(-\sum_n\psi_n)\), and can a joint zeroth-order oracle achieve it with approximate economic guarantees? A theorem package can begin with the two-coupling impossibility for marginal-only messages, then give a positive construction using synchronized joint samples (or dependence certificates) and a tail-externality price. Q original quadratic local payment gradient matches separable KKT conditions (Q lines 239--320); aggregate CVaR generally has distribution-dependent cross-agent tail effects, so the unchanged LMI payment is not enough. P local estimator remains useful only after changing its query model to paired joint samples. The earlier nonsmooth-VI and bias analysis remains a secondary layer, not the main novelty.

Qualification: the two-coupling example proves non-identifiability of aggregate CVaR values from local marginals; to prove different optimal allocations, the construction must make the dependence coupling decision-dependent so that the aggregate-CVaR optimizer changes while all local oracle laws remain identical. Also, aggregate CVaR is a normative alternative, not automatically the correct social objective: if welfare is explicitly the sum of individual risk preferences, Q local-CVaR substitution targets the intended objective and there is no diversification error. Any paper must state which planner semantics it adopts.

Final position after reading through #36: replace the literal P-inside-Q splice with the aggregate-risk information question in #35. The leading negative result is marginal-oracle indistinguishability under different dependence couplings; the positive research task is to augment Q with minimal joint-tail information and analyze a paired-sample zeroth-order game method. Retain the local-CVaR nonsmooth mechanism and biased-oracle bounds as the alternative branch when the normative target is a sum of individual tail utilities. Unresolved: a decision-dependent indistinguishability example with different optimal allocations; whether Q quadratic payments can encode the aggregate tail externality or require a richer payment family; the minimal synchronized sampling/message model; generalized-KKT uniqueness and full-message convergence; and prior-art novelty, which was not searched externally.
